title: Maximize Number of Subsequences in a String
statement:
You get two strings of lowercase English letters: `text`, and `pattern`, which has exactly two characters. Insert exactly one character into `text`; it must be `pattern[0]` or `pattern[1]`, and it may go anywhere, including before the first or after the last character.

Return the largest number of times `pattern` can occur as a subsequence of the new string. An occurrence is a pair of positions `i < j` whose characters are `pattern[0]` and `pattern[1]` in that order (a subsequence keeps some characters in their original order and drops the rest). The answer can exceed 32-bit range.
constraints: text and pattern contain only lowercase English letters
notes:
## Intuition

Trying every insertion point for both letters and recounting is O(n²) or worse. Two observations make it O(n). First, the number of occurrences already in `text` can be counted in one pass: every `pattern[1]` pairs with each `pattern[0]` seen before it. Second, where to insert is obvious. A new `pattern[0]` placed at the very start pairs with every `pattern[1]` in the text, and a new `pattern[1]` placed at the very end pairs with every `pattern[0]`. No other spot does better, so the bonus is simply the larger of the two letter counts.

## Approach

1. Let `first` and `second` be the two pattern letters; start `firstCount`, `secondCount` and `pairs` at 0.
2. For each character `c` of `text`: if it equals `second`, add `firstCount` to `pairs` (each earlier `first` forms a new pair) and increment `secondCount`.
3. Then, if `c` equals `first`, increment `firstCount`. Checking `second` before `first` keeps a letter from pairing with itself when both pattern letters are the same.
4. Return `pairs + max(firstCount, secondCount)`.

## Example 1, step by step

`text = "abdcdbc"`, `pattern = "ac"`. The `a` at index 0 makes `firstCount = 1`. The `c` at index 3 adds `1` to `pairs` and makes `secondCount = 1`; the `c` at index 6 adds another `1`, so `pairs = 2` and `secondCount = 2`. The answer is `2 + max(1, 2) = 4`: an extra `a` at the front pairs with both `c`s.

## Complexity

- Time: O(n): one pass over `text`.
- Space: O(1): three counters.

## Pitfalls

- When `pattern[0] == pattern[1]`, a character must not pair with itself; update `pairs` before `firstCount`.
- The count can reach about 5·10⁹ for a length of 10⁵, which overflows 32-bit integers in Java or C; use a 64-bit type.
- Count `pattern[1]` even when `pattern[0]` never appears: the inserted `pattern[0]` can still pair with all of them.

## Variables

| Name | Meaning |
|---|---|
| `first`, `second` | `pattern[0]` and `pattern[1]` |
| `firstCount` | how many `first` letters have been seen so far |
| `secondCount` | how many `second` letters have been seen so far |
| `pairs` | occurrences of `pattern` already in `text` |
| `c` | the current character |

narration.2: The letter that must come first in an occurrence.
narration.3: The letter that must come second.
narration.6: pairs counts the occurrences already present in text.
narration.8: Walk through text once, left to right.
narration.9: A second letter completes a pair with every first letter seen before it...
narration.10: ...so add all of them to pairs.
narration.11: Also count it: an inserted first letter at the front would pair with it.
narration.13: Count first letters after the pairing step, so an equal letter never pairs with itself.
narration.14: One more first letter is now available for later second letters.
narration.17: Insert at the best end: a first letter at the front gains secondCount, a second letter at the back gains firstCount.
